articles.title: Firms should publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law, says PM
articles.summary: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
articles.content:
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

Financial Secretary to the Treasury James Murray told the BBC "this is an important common sense reform".

Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, he said pay "shouldn't be a guessing game" and acknowledged the frustration some might feel when applying for jobs.

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

This policy has broad societal benefits by promoting fairness and equality in employment, backed by strong public support and aligned with similar EU measures. The article provides sufficient context about the policy's potential impact on reducing youth inactivity and pay disputes.

This idea was supported by 94% of people who took part in a recent consultation. Officials say this change will help jobseekers, especially young people who are not in education, employment, or training (called "Neet"), by giving them clear information up front.

**Impact** – Sharing salary information openly can help stop unfair pay differences between workers. It also means people can feel more confident asking about pay if they think they are being treated unfairly. This move is expected to reduce confusion and disagreements about wages and encourage more people to apply for jobs that fit their needs. Similar rules are already being introduced in the European Union.

**What's next step** – The government will review feedback from the consultation and prepare the final report on youth inactivity soon. After that, they will likely create laws or rules to make salary transparency a requirement for employers across the UK.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Requiring salary details in job adverts aims to make job searching clearer and fairer, helping people find suitable work and reducing pay discrimination.

articles.title: The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing […]
The post The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time.

Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving, sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch.

National organizations with locations near you

These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in.

Feeding America

Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent.

Meals on Wheels

Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit.

The Salvation Army

The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice.

Operation Turkey

Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit.

Feed My Starving Children

Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of.

Toys for Tots

Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs.

Goodwill

Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in.

United Way

United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter.

Local options that don’t require a national signup

Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome.

If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work.

The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park.

If you can’t leave the house

Gift-a-Family

Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time.

Homefront America

Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families.

Support Our Troops

Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way.

One thing to know before you go

Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush!

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

articles.title: Venezuela welcomes opposition leader María Corina Machado home
articles.summary: Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado returned to Caracas in a massive celebration after months in hiding and exile, sparking deep hope and sharp questions about the country’s political future.
articles.content:
Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile. The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country. She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro. Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S. President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:

Estoy aquí. Con ustedes — María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026

I am here. With you all.

Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans. Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.

A different country

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.

Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process. Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.

Yet, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures. Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different. There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.

People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time. After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.

Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her. She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen. On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.

At one point, two patrols from the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) passed by. The people closest to the highway lane began shouting at them, “Get out, get out!” but no one blocked their path or touched their doors or windows and the patrols continued on their way. Known as Venezuela’s political police, the DGCIM was one of the bodies singled out for 2024’s repressive post-election measures, in which more than 2,300 people were detained.

New uncertainties

Asked about the possible aftermaths of Machado’s return, caravan participants shared differing perspectives. Veterinarian Marianna Torres had no doubts about the order of things: Venezuela must have presidential elections, and soon, but not with the same electoral institutions that have permitted electoral fraud in the past. For her, all branches of power are corrupt and must be cleaned up before any election.

She also urged people looking at Venezuela from the outside to stop listening solely to politicians and pay attention to what “everyday Venezuelans” — the ones who know there are still political prisoners, human rights violations, and government authoritarian control — are saying.

Gabriela Santander, a publicist and activist for the Encuentro Ciudadano party, thought almost the opposite regarding the timeline. Stressing that she had been waiting for this day for months, since before Machado left, she believes that going to vote now, without an independent electoral arbiter or an impartial Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ), would be falling into a trap. Her deadline is concrete: if a new Electoral National Center is not in place by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the time to put on pressure will arrive.

Santander suspects that behind Machado’s return — which she believes could not have happened without Washington's approval — are agreements that no one has disclosed, especially since Rubio confirmed that his government had negotiated her return with the interim government “many weeks ago.” What Santander noticed the night of the caravan, however, was something more important: people had been on the highway for more than four hours and authorities had not tried to detain them.

Attorney Joyffer Briceño took a pragmatic view of the situation. While he sees Machado as the leader of those who want to restore the country’s institutions, he does not mistake emotion for change. “Those who hold power today are the same ones who were part of the crisis for years,” he explained. “I want something less abstract than an economic growth figure; I want the improvement to be felt in the pockets of every Venezuelan.”

For José Gregorio Rodríguez Cham, Machado’s arrival carries a different weight. His father, Julio Rodríguez Salazar, is a political prisoner, so he attended the event with other relatives to continue demanding the release of the 322 political prisoners who, according to Foro Penal, remain detained. He believes that new elections would be different because of the oversight of the United States, but he does not deny that the repressive apparatus in Venezuela remains intact, and that dismantling it will take time. What he years for in the coming months are elections and freedom, starting with that of his family.

Raquel Bugallo, a merchant in Caracas, remains somewhat suspicious of outside help. She believes that the international humanitarian aid Venezuela expected was overshadowed by economic interests, and that oil has been both Venezuela’s greatest wealth and “worst curse.” While she didn’t reject Rubio's call for understanding among all sectors, she did attach a condition: finding common ground, as long as the country can move forward. Her message to the international community was the shortest of the night: “If you are not going to help us, don’t get in our way.”

The day after Machado’s return, Delcy Rodríguez quipped that “the show could have been avoided.” Meanwhile, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights reminded the Venezuelan state of its obligation to guarantee the life, integrity, and political rights of the leader. Between November 11 and 15, the dialogue table will meet again, for the first time with Machado inside the country.

In the meantime, Venezuelans can savour the feeling of having spent hours on the streets without that familiar fear of repression. While repressive bodies were still present, passing in patrols through the crowd, on October 25, 2026, with Machado waving from the back of a pickup truck, the people stared back at them and told them to go, which must have felt something like progress.

The large public celebration and ongoing political dialogue indicate meaningful societal impact and potential for democratic restoration, benefiting the broader Venezuelan population.

Su presencia dio esperanza a muchos venezolanos que desean elecciones justas y mejores instituciones. A diferencia de protestas anteriores con pocos participantes, este evento reunió a familias y ciudadanos comunes, mostrando un interés más amplio en el cambio. Todo ocurrió de manera pacífica a pesar de la presencia de fuerzas de seguridad.

**Próximos pasos** – Machado participará en las conversaciones políticas programadas para noviembre, donde se discutirán el futuro del país, las elecciones y los derechos humanos. Muchos venezolanos esperan que estas charlas conduzcan a reformas reales, como reglas electorales imparciales y la liberación de presos políticos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El regreso seguro de María Corina Machado a Venezuela tras su exilio representa un momento esperanzador para el diálogo político y la participación ciudadana en busca de un cambio democrático.

articles.title: Unmarried Chinese women are rewriting the marriage script
articles.summary: Some unmarried Chinese women are actively challenging the social stigma associated with being “leftover women” by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or reframing the discussion altogether.
articles.content:
On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.

For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.

These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a meaningful social shift where unmarried Chinese women actively challenge stigmatizing cultural norms and family pressures around marriage. This represents a significant step toward gender equality and personal freedom in a large society, with detailed examples of how women reframe and resist traditional expectations, fostering empowerment and broader societal dialogue.
articles.personality_title: Unmarried Chinese women challenge old marriage expectations
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In China, many unmarried women have faced the label "shengnü," meaning "leftover women," a term that suggests they are past the right age for marriage. This label has caused social pressure and family expectations to marry, especially for educated urban women in their late twenties and thirties.

**What happened** – Recently, fewer people use the harsh term "shengnü." Instead, new words and conversations have appeared on social media where women openly discuss the pressure to marry and their fears about marriage itself. Some women share stories about how moving away or ignoring family pressure helps them find freedom. Others have taken the negative label and turned it into something positive by calling themselves "victorious women," focusing on personal success instead of marriage.

**Impact** – This change shows that many unmarried women in China are no longer accepting old ideas that marriage defines their worth. By talking openly about their experiences and supporting each other online, they challenge family pressures and society’s expectations. This helps more people think differently about marriage and women’s choices.

**What's next step** – As more women continue to share their stories and create new ways to talk about marriage and independence, society may slowly change its views. This could lead to greater acceptance of different life choices for women and less pressure to marry by a certain age.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Unmarried Chinese women are reshaping how society sees marriage by refusing stigma and choosing personal freedom and success instead.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les femmes chinoises célibataires défient les attentes traditionnelles du mariage
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Chine, de nombreuses femmes célibataires ont été qualifiées de « shengnü », ce qui signifie « femmes restantes », un terme suggérant qu'elles ont dépassé l'âge idéal pour se marier. Cette étiquette a créé une pression sociale et familiale, surtout pour les femmes urbaines et instruites dans la trentaine.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Récemment, ce terme dur est moins utilisé. De nouveaux mots et discussions apparaissent sur les réseaux sociaux, où les femmes parlent ouvertement de la pression au mariage et de leurs craintes. Certaines racontent comment déménager ou ignorer la pression familiale leur apporte de la liberté. D'autres transforment l'étiquette négative en positif en se qualifiant de « femmes victorieuses », en valorisant leur réussite personnelle plutôt que le mariage.

**Impact** – Ce changement montre que beaucoup de femmes célibataires en Chine refusent l'idée que le mariage définit leur valeur. En partageant leurs expériences et en se soutenant en ligne, elles remettent en cause les attentes familiales et sociales. Cela incite davantage de personnes à revoir leur regard sur le mariage et les choix des femmes.

**Prochaine étape** – Au fur et à mesure que ces femmes continuent à partager leurs histoires et à créer de nouveaux discours sur le mariage et l'indépendance, la société pourrait évoluer. Cela pourrait conduire à une plus grande acceptation de différents modes de vie et à moins de pression pour se marier avant un certain âge.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les femmes chinoises célibataires redéfinissent la vision du mariage en refusant la stigmatisation et en choisissant la liberté personnelle et la réussite.
articles.personality_title_es: Mujeres solteras chinas desafían las expectativas tradicionales del matrimonio
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En China, muchas mujeres solteras han sido llamadas "shengnü", que significa "mujeres sobrantes", un término que sugiere que ya pasaron la edad ideal para casarse. Esta etiqueta ha generado presión social y familiar, especialmente para mujeres urbanas y educadas en sus treinta años.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, se usa menos el término duro "shengnü". Aparecen nuevas palabras y conversaciones en redes sociales donde las mujeres hablan abiertamente sobre la presión para casarse y sus miedos al matrimonio. Algunas cuentan cómo mudarse o ignorar la presión familiar les da libertad. Otras transforman la etiqueta negativa en positiva llamándose "mujeres victoriosas", enfocándose en el éxito personal en lugar del matrimonio.

**Impacto** – Este cambio muestra que muchas mujeres solteras en China ya no aceptan que el matrimonio defina su valor. Al compartir sus experiencias y apoyarse en línea, desafían las expectativas familiares y sociales. Esto hace que más personas reconsideren el matrimonio y las decisiones de las mujeres.

**Próximo paso** – A medida que más mujeres continúan compartiendo sus historias y creando nuevas formas de hablar sobre el matrimonio y la independencia, la sociedad podría cambiar poco a poco. Esto podría llevar a una mayor aceptación de diferentes opciones de vida y menos presión para casarse a cierta edad.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las mujeres solteras chinas están cambiando la forma en que la sociedad ve el matrimonio al rechazar el estigma y elegir la libertad personal y el éxito.
